#9778. A Payment Webhook Should Not Grant the Same Purchase Twice

When a learning platform sells a digital resource, the interesting part of payment integration is often the second notification.

The first confirmed payment can grant access. A repeated notification must not grant it again, record another collection, or create a second purchase event for advertising analytics.

I am Hassan Essam, founder of Snuhy, an Egyptian learning and digital services platform. This is a small design note about a rule we use when defining payment behavior: count a sale after confirmed payment, and preserve one identity for that sale across retries.

The example below is explanatory pseudocode, not an extract from our production code or a complete payment integration.

An integration can have at least three identifiers:

Deduplicating only the event ID is insufficient if two distinct notifications describe the same payment. Deduplicating only the order ID can also be wrong when an order legitimately supports multiple collections.

Choose the business key for the action. An access grant might be unique per order and product. A collection should use the confirmed payment identity. An advertising purchase event needs the identity of the sale it represents.

A unique constraint is part of correctness here. Two workers can both pass an application-level “does this exist?” check before either inserts a record. The database needs to reject the conflicting duplicate.

The exact keys and transitions depend on the payment provider and business model. An installment collection, a full purchase, and a refund should not be forced into one event merely because all three involve money.

An outbox helps avoid a committed payment with a missing notification job. It does not eliminate the uncertainty of an external request.

A provider might accept a request just before the worker loses its connection. Retrying without reconciliation can duplicate the external effect. Use the destination's supported idempotency or event-deduplication mechanism, retain the result, and distinguish known failure from uncertain acceptance.

For purchase measurement, use a stable sale identity. If browser and server both report the same sale, configure the destination's deduplication mechanism consistently. Also check measurement consent before enqueueing or sending; confirmation of payment is not itself marketing consent.

These checks should use isolated fixtures, fake external services, and test-provider facilities. There is no need to create fake revenue in a live financial ledger to prove that retries are handled.

The customer-facing consequence is straightforward: a repeated technical notification should not look like a second purchase. Achieving that requires each downstream action to have a defined business identity and an explicit retry policy.

Disclosure: I am the founder of Snuhy. This article was drafted with AI assistance from recorded project requirements and is presented as a conceptual design example. It makes no claim of a measured conversion uplift or a provider-certified implementation.

#9776. A free OpenAPI diff that never uploads your spec

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at graphwake.com

Pasting an internal API spec into a website is a hard sell. The spec lists every endpoint and every field, and sometimes the hosts behind them, so you want to know where it goes.

We build Graphwake, which tells the teams that consume an API when a change in its OpenAPI spec is about to break them. Along the way we built a free OpenAPI diff where the comparison runs in your browser tab. Paste the old and the new spec, choose two files or give two URLs, and it shows every change that can break a client. Free, no sign-up.

A breaking change is one that can make an existing client fail. These come first in every result:

A new optional field, endpoint or response code breaks no one. Those are listed separately, out of your way.

The "Try an example" result: 3 breaking changes, each under the line it comes from.

A file you choose is read in the tab. A URL is fetched by your browser straight from that address, so that server has to allow it (CORS). We never receive the spec, the file or the URL. If you want to check, keep the Network tab of your DevTools open while you compare.

Two limits come with running in the browser. A spec can be up to 10 MB of text, but very large specs, a few megabytes of YAML, can take longer than the 20 seconds the browser check allows; the result then says so. And references to other files ($ref: ./schemas.yaml) can't be followed, so bundle the spec into one file first.

A diff tells you what changed. Whether the change is safe depends on something else: who calls this endpoint? The author of the change usually doesn't know, and nobody keeps the list.

Example: the same kind of breaking change, sent only to the teams that call the endpoint.

Do you paste internal specs into online tools today, or is that off limits where you work?

#9775. How to Modernize Bank Without Taking Its Payment Systems Offline

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Senior Solution Architect, Diebold Nixdorf. 16 years in secure payments, ATM/POS and digital banking. MSc AI candidate.

Every bank I have worked with has a system nobody wants to touch.

Sometimes it is a mainframe core banking platform written in COBOL. Sometimes it is a card switch that has been processing ISO 8583 messages reliably for twenty years. Sometimes it is a batch file job that runs at 2 a.m. and that exactly one engineer understands. These systems are old, but they are not broken. They move real money every second.

And yet the business wants mobile apps, open banking APIs, real-time payments and cloud analytics. The question is never "should we modernize?" The question is "how do we modernize without taking the ATM network offline on a Friday payday?"

After roughly sixteen years building ATM, POS and digital banking middleware for banks across the Middle East, Asia and Europe, here is what I have seen actually work.

The tempting plan is to replace the old core in one program. It rarely goes well. Large core replacements have a long public history of delays, outages and customers locked out of their accounts. The reasons repeat:

The alternative is incremental modernization. Less exciting, far more survivable.

Before writing new code, build an inventory of every point where systems talk to each other: protocols (ISO 8583, SWIFT MT/MX, ISO 20022, flat files, SOAP, proprietary TCP), message volumes, peak times, and who owns each interface.

In most banks this map reveals a "spaghetti" of point-to-point links. The ATM switch talks directly to the core. The mobile app calls a SOAP service that calls another SOAP service that writes to a shared database. Every new channel added another direct connection.

You cannot modernize what you have not mapped. You also cannot secure it.

The single most valuable move is introducing a governed integration layer between channels and back-end systems. This can be an API gateway plus a payment middleware or message broker, depending on the flow.

With the layer in place, use the strangler fig pattern: move one business flow at a time from legacy to new, while the rest keeps running untouched.

For each flow, run the new path in shadow mode first: send traffic to both systems, compare results, and only switch over when mismatches are near zero. Keep the routing switch reversible for weeks, not hours.

Integration layers are where security quietly degrades. Patterns I see repeatedly:

This matters well beyond one bank. In the United States, CISA identifies financial services as critical infrastructure, and regulators such as the FFIEC and OCC have repeatedly flagged third-party and legacy integration risk. As U.S. banks connect older cores to real-time rails like the Federal Reserve's FedNow Service and to ISO 20022 messaging, the integration layer becomes the front line of payment security.

During migration, two systems may each believe they own the truth. Automate reconciliation between legacy and new ledgers daily at minimum, and in near real time for payment flows. Every mismatch is either a migration bug or a hidden business rule you did not know about. Both are worth finding before customers do.

Teams celebrate when the new system goes live and forget to decommission the old path. Two systems running forever means double the attack surface and double the cost. For each migrated flow, define:

Legacy banking systems are not the enemy. They are proof that something worked for decades. Modernization succeeds when it respects that, puts a disciplined integration layer between old and new, moves one flow at a time, and treats security and reconciliation as part of the design.

The banks that get this right do not make headlines. Their customers simply never notice the migration happened. That is the goal.

#9774. Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

Inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly new great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, Llama App (llama.cpp), and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

Similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

In this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Llama App lets you easily run and manage local language models on macOS (from the menu bar) or Windows (system tray). It’s built on llama.cpp, and by the same team. The app also provides a local OpenAI-compatible API for easy integration with coding agents, editors, and scripts.

#9773. Why I Chose Node.js Storage for Generated Images and Temporary Download Links

When an e-commerce app stores AI-generated images, the hard part is not writing bytes. It is moving large files to the right tenant without turning every download into an application-server transfer. Short answer: store private objects in object storage and mint a short-lived signed URL only when a user requests an export. That keeps the delivery path fast and leaves the vendor choice reversible.

For this exact workflow, Infrai is a reasonable first candidate when one REST credential should cover storage and the rest of a backend. The useful test is still throughput and replaceability, not a logo.

I care about time-to-first-call and the amount of glue a CLI needs. My first sketch put image data in a database and streamed it through Node.js. That was a bad boundary: exports competed with API traffic, and a retry could repeat a large upload. The useful boundary is an object key such as tenant_42/jobs/job_8f2/result.webp; the database owns who can see it, while storage owns the bytes.

Give each generated image a record containing user_id, prompt_id or job id, object key, MIME type, and size. That index is more dependable than trying to search object metadata. Before showing a download action, an object-head call can confirm that the key exists and report its current size. For a tenant export, authorize the user against the database record first, then create a URL with an expiry that matches the workflow.

Here is the small TypeScript client I use for the two calls in that path. It makes the HTTP method explicit, keeps the key out of source control, and backs off on rate limits. The presign operation is a request, not a public ACL; the resulting link is temporary.

The exact response envelope is part of the provider contract, so production code should validate payload.url before returning it. I would also make the database lookup the authorization gate; possession of an object key must never be treated as tenant access.

Large-file throughput shifts the bottleneck to upload and copy strategy. Keep the API server out of the data path where possible: have the worker write directly to the object store, then persist the metadata row. If a single image must appear under two prefixes (for example, a tenant folder and an audit export), use object copy rather than downloading and re-uploading the same bytes through Node.js. That is less glue and fewer opportunities to corrupt a transfer.

For a bursty catalog job, I would queue generation and export records, cap concurrent downloads per tenant, and measure object size before creating links. The queue should carry the tenant id, job id, key, MIME type, and expected size; workers can reject a stale record before touching storage, while a per-tenant semaphore prevents one catalog refresh from consuming every connection. My benchmark counters are boring on purpose: bytes written, presign latency, head latency, and completed links. A pretty dashboard cannot tell me whether a 200 MB export is starving checkout traffic.

S3-compatible APIs make the application boundary portable, but compatibility is not identical feature coverage. Here is the decision table I keep beside the migration checklist.

Infrai is worth trying when you want the storage workflow behind plain HTTP and already use other backend capabilities under the same credential. Its public discovery surface and runnable examples reduce SDK glue, and the storage contract is small enough to wrap behind an interface. That is the concrete portability play: my Node.js code depends on put, head, copy, and presign semantics, not on a vendor-specific object model.

The catch is real. Infrai has no public-read ACL, so it is not suitable for a permanent public image CDN or a static website that expects anonymous URLs. It also lacks object versioning and object lock; an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through those features. There is no If-Match conditional write, no automatic cross-region replication, and no cross-cloud bulk migration tool. Browser direct uploads need a CORS setup that the service does not expose as an independent route. Stick with S3 when you need those controls, or choose a specialist such as R2 when edge delivery is the primary concern.

Lifecycle rules have a one-day minimum, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule. Metadata is not server-searchable; list operations filter by prefix. Those are design constraints, not surprises to hide in a postmortem. Put retention and concurrency policy in your queue and database, and document a separate disaster-recovery copy if the product needs one.

Define a storage adapter whose public methods accept a tenant id and return an object key or signed URL. Store that key in your database, never in a URL column. During a provider move, copy objects, switch the adapter, and keep old links short-lived so the cutover window stays bounded. A copy route is useful here, but replication is still your responsibility.

I am not sure any single storage vendor wins every export workload; your mileage may vary with region, object size, and queue limits. The stable choice is the one you can replace without rewriting authorization and job tracking. For private AI images, that means object storage plus on-demand signed links, with throughput measured at the object boundary.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage contract and discovery examples at https://docs.infrai.cc.

#9772. 5 Types Of Brain-Affecting Drugs Still Prescribed Despite Safety Warnings

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

Five drug groups carry warnings for older adults, yet prescribing remains highest among those with dementia.

One in four older Americans with dementia is prescribed potentially inappropriate medicines that affect the brain and nervous system.

These drugs can increase the risk of confusion, falls and hospitalisation, particularly in people whose thinking and memory are already impaired.

Despite decades of warnings, people with cognitive impairment were more likely to receive these prescriptions than those with normal cognition.

The research examined five categories of medication flagged by prescribing guidelines for older adults:

Only antidepressants with strong anticholinergic properties were included in this category.

Anticholinergic medicines block acetylcholine, a chemical messenger involved in memory, learning and concentration.

Blocking its action can cause confusion and other unwanted effects, especially in older adults.

Benzodiazepines, which may be prescribed for anxiety or sleep problems, can cause excessive drowsiness and increase the risk of falls.

Some medicines also take longer to leave the body as people age, allowing their effects to persist or accumulate.

The researchers analysed survey information linked to medical insurance records from almost 4,900 Americans aged 65 and over.

They examined prescribing over nine years, counting prescriptions for at least four weeks’ supply.

Around 17 percent of people with normal cognition received at least one potentially inappropriate prescription, compared with almost 22 percent of those with cognitive impairment without dementia.

Among people with dementia, the proportion reached 25 percent.

Across the older adults studied, prescribing fell from around 20 percent at the beginning of the study period to 16 percent at the end.

Much of the decline reflected fewer prescriptions for benzodiazepines and Z-drug sleeping medicines.

However, prescribing rates for the other three drug groups did not change significantly.

By the final year, more than two-thirds of people receiving these potentially inappropriate prescriptions lacked a documented clinical reason for at least one of them.

A potentially inappropriate medicine can still be justified when its expected benefits outweigh its risks.

The practical question is whether each prescription remains suitable for the person taking it.

Dr Annie Yang, the study’s first author, emphasised the importance of patients and carers reviewing these medicines with their physicians:

“While CNS-active prescriptions may be appropriate in some cases, it is important for older patients or their caregivers to work closely with their physicians to ensure that these medications are appropriate to their cases.

When inappropriate, patients and their care teams should consider alternative treatments and consider whether it might be safe to taper or stop the medication.”

The study was published in JAMA (Yang et al., 2026).

#9771. MCP Tool Deprecation and Registry Lifecycle, Stage by Stage

Posted on Nov 22 • Originally published at powerduck.com

Quick answer: Retiring an MCP tool is a two-plane problem, not a delete action. The catalog controls whether agents can discover a tool; the backend controls whether a saved call still reaches it, and the two move independently. Run a staged lifecycle: mark the entry deprecated with a named replacement, keep the backend reachable through a fixed sunset window while logging who still calls it, remove the entry from discovery, then decommission the backend. Deleting first turns saved agents into hard failures with no pointer to the replacement.

An MCP deployment has a catalog plane and a runtime plane. The catalog is the list agents read at discovery; the runtime is the server and backend that answer a call. An entry can be hidden while the server keeps answering, and a server can be shut off while the entry stays listed, the worse case because an agent then discovers a tool it cannot call. Change both planes on purpose and in order.

Each state changes one plane at a time: active, deprecated while fully reachable, a sunset window that warns but keeps working, loss of catalog visibility, then backend decommission.

Keep the backend alive past catalog removal so an agent that cached the address still works. Shutting the backend off while the entry stays listed creates a dangling entry: discovery succeeds, the call fails, nothing signals a planned retirement.

Where the state lives depends on who runs the catalog. A managed registry supplies the states and marks, so deprecated and archived are platform fields the Hub renders to browsing agents, and the vendor sets the warning readers see. Your control ends at the platform's state machine; with no dated sunset field, you cannot add one through the API.

A self-hosted gateway puts routing and responses in your hands. You can emit machine-readable signals such as the Sunset header and a Deprecation header, keep custom stages, and count calls per retired route yourself. None of it is built in: the state store, warning logic, call logs, and the calendar that flips a stage are code you own and run.

Powerduck Cloud treats retirement as a state change rather than a delete: every edit keeps a version with diff and rollback, and pause, resume, and archive move a hosted entry without erasing its history, so an archived MCP server leaves the public Hub while its versions stay recoverable. The comparison hub sets this against the broader build-versus-buy trade-offs.

A catalog mark is a discovery-time signal, not a remote control. A saved prompt or long-running agent holds a tool name and often a direct address and does not re-read the catalog on every call, so marking an entry deprecated edits nothing already saved. That is why the deprecated stage needs a long window and call logs showing who still depends on the old name.

MCP defines no catalog-level lifecycle field, so deprecated and archived are platform conventions, not protocol guarantees the host enforces. HTTP warning headers help only when the caller reads them; a framework that ignores them sees a normal result until the backend goes dark. Verify through declining call counts rather than assuming the signal landed.

What is the difference between removing a tool from the registry and shutting the server down? Removing it from the catalog stops new discovery while saved calls can still reach a running backend. Shutting the server down makes every call fail. Keep the first ahead of the second so saved agents have a working window.

How long should the sunset window be? Long enough that call logs show no traffic to the old tool across a full usage cycle. There is no fixed number; tie the date to measured callers and name the replacement in the deprecated mark.

Can I just delete the entry and have agents switch on their own? No. Deleting produces a hard failure for anything that saved the name, and MCP has no field that rewrites a saved prompt. Mark, warn, and wait out a window first so the model has a named replacement to move to.

The registry lifecycle is mostly about not stranding existing callers. A clean retirement changes the catalog and backend separately, keeps the runtime alive through a measured sunset, and treats every deprecated mark as a signal the platform may not deliver. A managed registry gives you the states and marks; your own gateway gives you the headers and routing but leaves coordination on you. Delete last and verify with call logs, so no saved agent calls a tool that vanished without a pointer.

#9769. What Happens to Your Digital Accounts After a Chargeback?

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Your issuing bank will happily hand your 50 USD back. What the representative on the phone will rarely mention is that once those funds are clawed back, the merchant on the other side of the trade holds sweeping contractual rights over your account. When that merchant happens to run your cloud storage, your smart home, your decade-old gaming library, or your daily ride to work, a minor billing victory can turn into a painful digital lockout overnight.

After 25 years in traditional banking, I cringe every time I hear social media finance gurus repeat their favorite piece of lazy advice: "If customer support gives you a hard time about a refund, just call your credit card company and file a chargeback." People treat the bank dispute button like a VIP customer service hotline. It is nothing of the sort. Inside the plumbing of global card rails, a chargeback is a forced financial extraction. You are asking your bank to reach directly into a merchant's settlement balance, pull the cash back over the card network, trigger a punitive dispute fee, and log a blemish against their compliance metrics with Visa or Mastercard.

Do that to a neighborhood dry cleaner and they might ban you from the shop. Do that to Apple, Google, Sony, Valve, Microsoft, Amazon, or Uber over a 20 USD subscription renewal, and you are rolling the dice with automated risk engines that control far more than a single receipt. At best, your profile gets hit with an unpaid balance lock or a payment verification hold; at worst, if the platform flags the reversal as payment abuse or unauthorized activity, you can win a 20 USD battle at your bank only to lose access to thousands of dollars in purchased media, connected devices, or cloud workflows.

To understand why tech platforms treat bank disputes so seriously, you have to understand the legal and operational chasm between a refund and a chargeback. During a standard refund, the merchant voluntarily pushes money back to your card over the payment rails. During a chargeback, your issuing bank forcibly reverses the transaction through the card network's dispute machinery, bypassing the merchant's checkout support entirely.

Consumers often assume that when their bank rules in their favor, the case is closed and the merchant has to respect the verdict. That is a costly misunderstanding of how commercial law works. Your bank adjudicates whether you owe the money on your monthly card statement; the tech platform adjudicates whether you are allowed to use its servers under its terms of service. When you pull the trigger on a dispute, your money and your account standing can quickly start moving in opposite directions.

In the United States, consumer banking protections are remarkably strong on paper. For credit cards, the Fair Credit Billing Act (implemented through Regulation Z) gives you the legal right to challenge billing errors and unauthorized charges. According to the CFPB's official credit card dispute rules, as long as you send written notice within 60 calendar days after the error first appeared on your statement, the card issuer must investigate and pause collection on the disputed charge (often issuing a temporary credit) while the case plays out. Debit cards carry separate protections for unauthorized electronic fund transfers under Regulation E's error resolution framework.

Here is the catch that catches everyday users off guard. Regulation Z and Regulation E bind your bank, not the merchant. Zero federal statutes force a private corporation to keep extending services to a customer who just reversed a settled payment.

Worse yet, consumers increasingly lean on bank disputes for what the payments industry calls first-party fraud, or "friendly fraud." According to Mastercard's 2026 chargeback outlook, global chargeback volume is projected to reach 334 million disputes annually by 2028, while merchants report that 21% of chargebacks are linked to first-party fraud, ranging from unrecognized or forgotten charges to intentional misuse of the dispute process. Separate Mastercard-sponsored research with Javelin found that for 75% of disputes, consumers go straight to their card issuer without contacting the merchant first. Because issuing banks often find it cheaper to credit small disputes automatically than to investigate them manually, cardholders get lulled into thinking the tactic is consequence-free.

Of course, if a thief steals your physical wallet or hijacks your account, you must call your bank immediately and freeze the card. My warning here applies to using bank disputes as a casual shortcut to resolve everyday billing friction with ecosystems you cannot afford to lose.

If you want to know why a trillion-dollar company will freeze purchases or restrict an account over a 19.99 USD charge, stop looking at the customer support department and look at the treasury and risk desk. Every card transaction travels along a four-party rail: you (the cardholder), your issuing bank (such as Chase or Capital One), the card network (Visa or Mastercard), and the merchant's acquiring bank or payment processor (such as Stripe, Adyen, or J.P. Morgan Merchant Services).

When you initiate a chargeback, a costly chain reaction hits the merchant's back office:

Put yourself in the shoes of a platform risk officer looking at that math. A customer who files a 20 USD chargeback has just inflicted over 100 USD in combined direct and operational losses on the company. From a pure risk-management standpoint, letting an account rack up bank reversals unchecked makes zero financial sense.

The direct fees are only half the story. The deeper reason merchants aggressively police chargebacks is card network compliance enforcement. Visa and Mastercard track dispute and fraud ratios across every merchant portfolio on their rails.

In recent years, Visa overhauled its legacy compliance rules and consolidated five separate fraud and dispute tracks into a single framework: the Visa Acquirer Monitoring Program (VAMP). Under the official VAMP threshold schedule, Visa calculates a merchant's monthly ratio by combining TC40 fraud notices and TC15 non-fraud disputes divided by total settled card-not-present VisaNet transactions, with the U.S. Excessive Merchant threshold tightening to 1.5% (alongside at least 1,500 monthly combined fraud and dispute notices) in April 2026. Even if a merchant fights a chargeback and wins, that dispute still counts toward their monthly monitoring ratio.

Mastercard enforces a parallel framework called the Excessive Chargeback Program (ECP). As outlined in Stripe's card network monitoring guide, crossing both the 1.5% rate and 100-chargeback monthly count places a merchant into official remediation, with escalating monthly fines kicking in from the second consecutive month unless the ratio drops back below threshold. Payment processors simultaneously protect themselves from elevated dispute activity by holding a portion of a merchant's payouts in fixed or rolling reserves, as detailed in Stripe's merchant reserve policies.

Crossing a Visa or Mastercard monitoring threshold does not automatically terminate a merchant or blacklist the business overnight; the programs are built around mandatory remediation plans and escalating fees first. However, if a smaller vendor fails to bring its dispute levels down in time, the card network can eventually stop processing its payments, or its acquiring bank may terminate the account. As documented in Stripe's guide to terminated merchant files, once an acquirer terminates a merchant that meets specific network reporting criteria, such as Mastercard's MATCH Reason Code 04 (exceeding a 1% monthly Mastercard chargeback ratio and 5,000 USD in chargebacks within the same calendar month) or Visa's VMSS thresholds, the acquirer must report the business to those five-year high-risk databases, making it nearly impossible to open a new card-processing account elsewhere.

Even for giants like Sony, Apple, or Amazon, keeping ratios clean across dozens of regional merchant descriptors requires tight automated controls. Depending on how their fraud models classify a reversal, their systems will either lock new spending until the unpaid balance is cleared or quarantine the account for a security review.

Platforms do not react identically to every chargeback, and it helps to separate routine billing enforcement from worst-case account bans. Routinely, a single reversed payment creates an unpaid balance on your profile, revokes the specific item you disputed, or pauses new purchases until you settle the tab or verify your card. Contractually, however, every major tech ecosystem reserves broad authority to suspend or terminate accounts, and when an automated fraud model classifies a chargeback as unauthorized activity or payment abuse, the blast radius can hit your entire digital profile.

Gaming platforms enforce some of the strictest automated chargeback rules in the consumer economy, though each handles the boundary between a single revoked purchase and a full account lock differently.

Sony leaves very little wiggle room in its public rules. Under the PlayStation Network account debt and suspension policy, because a bank reversal can signal suspected fraud or an account takeover, Sony suspends the PSN account (or console) to investigate, displaying error codes WS-37368-7 or WS-116367-4 and restricting access to online services. If there was no lawful right to a refund, your PSN profile remains suspended until you repay the owed balance through Sony's recovery form, cutting you off from PlayStation Store purchases, online multiplayer, and PSN-authenticated features in the meantime.

Microsoft separates baseline chargeback handling from fraud enforcement across Xbox and Windows services. While Microsoft provides an official Xbox digital game refund portal for standard refund requests, bypassing Microsoft via your bank triggers Section 9.g of the Microsoft Services Agreement: Microsoft deems you to have canceled the service as of the original payment date and is authorized to immediately cancel that service and revoke the content provided for that payment. That is the routine baseline. However, if Xbox's risk systems determine that a chargeback or refund pattern crosses into fraudulent marketplace theft, Xbox Safety enforcement can escalate to temporary or permanent account and console bans, and Section 4.b.iv of the Services Agreement warns that permanent closure can forfeit your content licenses, memberships, and Microsoft account balances.

Think about how much of your daily digital routine runs through your Apple Account (formerly Apple ID). Under the Apple Media Services Terms and Conditions, you remain personally liable for any uncollected amounts, and Apple reserves broad authority to suspend or terminate access to its services or your Apple Account if you breach the agreement.

In everyday practice, Apple's documentation points to two distinct tiers of friction. If a failed or reversed payment simply leaves an unpaid order on your profile, Apple's unpaid balance support guide states that you might be unable to make new purchases, download free apps, or use subscriptions (and as noted in Apple's Mac App Store troubleshooting guide, an unpaid order can also block you from downloading or updating apps). In these routine unpaid-balance cases, manual intervention is not required: you can clear the balance yourself by adding a new valid payment method, which Apple charges automatically, or by redeeming an Apple Gift Card and applying the credit to the unpaid order in your purchase history.

However, if a chargeback or repeated billing dispute triggers an anti-fraud lock that disables your purchasing privileges outright, self-service card updates will no longer fix the problem. As shown in Apple's disabled Media & Purchases recovery guide, seeing the alert that your Media & Purchases account has been disabled means you have to request reactivation directly through Apple Support.

Google routes consumer and business billing through a shared hub: your Google Payments profile. As explained in Google's payments center documentation, that profile stores the cards, receipts, and recurring subscriptions behind Google Play, YouTube, Google One storage, hardware orders, and business tools.

A consumer chargeback does not automatically wipe out your Google Account or shut off Gmail on the spot. Instead, under the Google Pay and Google Payments U.S. Terms and Google's declined-transaction rules, when unusual or suspicious payment activity flags your payments profile, Google can block new purchases until you complete identity and payment verification, which may involve confirming a 6-digit temporary charge code or uploading images of a government ID and the payment card. If you also run ad campaigns on that account, Google Ads' billing suspension policy explicitly warns that instructing your bank to reverse a legitimate ad balance may result in your Google Ads account being paused or suspended.

For everyday users, the real danger of an unresolved payments-profile lock is the delayed domino effect on cloud storage. Under Google One's renewal and cancellation policies, if auto-renewal fails on your storage plan, Google provides a seven-day grace period to update your payment information. If a locked payments profile or unresolved billing dispute keeps your plan from renewing past that window and your usage sits above the free 15 GB quota, your Google Account stays accessible, but Google Photos stops backing up videos and pictures, Google Drive blocks new uploads and Workspace file creation, and Gmail stops sending and receiving messages, returning incoming emails to the sender. Leave an account over quota for two years or longer, and Google states your content may be deleted.

Amazon is no longer just a retailer that ships cardboard boxes to your porch; it also runs media libraries and smart-home devices tied to the same login. On routine marketplace disputes, Amazon's A-to-z Guarantee rules explicitly note that filing a credit card chargeback disqualifies that order from A-to-z Guarantee refund coverage, and ordinary payment declines usually just pause pending orders until you supply another card.

The stakes jump sharply, however, if a reversed charge or disputed card causes Amazon's risk models to flag your profile for unusual payment activity. Under Amazon's Conditions of Use, the company reserves broad discretion to refuse service or terminate accounts. More specifically, Amazon's Account on Hold policy states in plain English that when unusual payment activity triggers a temporary security hold on your account, your access to all Amazon services is also placed on hold during the review, explicitly listing Amazon Prime, Amazon Music, Kindle, and devices like Alexa and Ring. Until you sign into Amazon's secure portal and submit its verification form with the requested supporting attachments, your shopping account and connected digital services stay frozen together.

Uber illustrates a similar single-wallet bottleneck in daily transit and food delivery. Under Uber's U.S. Terms of Use, Uber retains sole discretion to deny access to or terminate any of its services at any time. In day-to-day operations, when a failed or reversed payment leaves an unpaid balance on your account, Uber's rider pending-amount rules and the matching Uber Eats outstanding-charge policy warn that you may be unable to request a ride or place a food order until you settle the pending charge in the app with a valid payment method (or arrange cash payment where supported).

Stepping back and looking at this friction through the lens of payment architecture reveals a striking irony. For decades, traditional bankers criticized cryptocurrency protocols because on-chain transactions are final and irreversible, whereas legacy credit cards offer consumer reversibility.

Yet in practice, credit card settlement finality is an illusion that encourages digital feudalism. When you swipe a Visa card, the merchant receives provisional funds within a couple of business days, but the transaction lacks true finality for months while card-network dispute windows remain open. Because centralized platforms cannot fully trust the finality of legacy fiat payment rails, they protect their balance sheets by tying your digital identity, subscriptions, and device ecosystems to a single revocable login.

In the crypto and Web3 world, we live by a simple rule: not your keys, not your coins. If you leave your digital assets on a centralized exchange, you do not hold bearer Bitcoin or stablecoins; you hold a revocable database entry that the exchange can freeze the moment a compliance or billing review flares up.

The exact same custody trap governs Web2 walled gardens. Not your servers, not your files. Even when you click the purchase button on an e-book, Amazon's Kindle Store terms of use explicitly state that digital content is licensed to you, not sold. When you bundle your primary email address, your cloud drive, your smart-home cameras, and thousands of dollars of revocable media licenses inside the same single sign-on profile that processes your credit card, you hand the platform enormous leverage. Your bank can force the merchant to return 50 USD, and the merchant retains the contractual power to freeze your billing profile, halt subscriptions, or, in severe enforcement cases, cut off access to thousands of dollars in licensed media.

In commercial banking, putting all of your operational liquidity and custody inside a single counterparty that can freeze your operations over a minor billing dispute is called concentration risk. No competent corporate treasurer would allow it, yet everyday consumers build their digital lives that way by default.

If you want to protect your money from bad billing without handing Big Tech unnecessary leverage over your accounts, follow these five operational rules.

If an unfamiliar storefront scams you on a pair of shoes from a random social media ad, file a chargeback without hesitation. However, if you are fighting a 30 USD charge from Apple, Google, Amazon, Sony, or Valve, treat the bank dispute button as a last resort. Exhaust the platform's internal refund escalation channels, reach out to executive customer relations, or file a formal complaint with the Better Business Bureau or your state Attorney General's consumer protection division first. Track your 60-day statutory bank deadline on the calendar so you never forfeit your legal rights under Regulation Z or Regulation E, but push the merchant to resolve the billing error internally whenever an essential account is on the line.

The cleanest way to win a billing dispute is to stop an unwanted charge at the authorization gate before the money ever settles. Once a charge settles, reversing it through your bank creates a chargeback; stopping an unwanted renewal at authorization simply triggers a routine "payment declined, please update your billing method" notice.

If you have thousands of dollars invested in a PlayStation, Steam, Xbox, or Apple library, leaving a live credit card or PayPal billing agreement on file means an accidental click, a child's in-game purchase, or a forgotten renewal can quickly turn into a high-stakes billing mess.

Instead, fund those wallets with prepaid store gift cards purchased from reputable retailers and remove live cards where possible. That way, the platform cannot pull more than the prepaid balance sitting in your wallet. Keep one practical rule in mind: under Apple's payment method removal policy, you must keep at least one payment method on file if you maintain active subscriptions like iCloud+, owe an unpaid balance, or serve as a Family Sharing organizer with purchase sharing enabled. Even then, keeping your Apple Account funded with gift cards helps ensure your prepaid balance absorbs routine charges before a backup card is touched.

Stop using the same Google or Apple account that holds your tax returns, family photo archives, and two-factor authentication recovery emails to test sketchy app trials or shared household entertainment. Build an air gap between your core infrastructure and your discretionary spending. Keep your primary email and cloud storage on a clean, dedicated account paid by a reliable card used strictly for storage infrastructure, and maintain a separate secondary account for media purchases, trials, and gaming.

Never confuse cloud syncing with an independent backup. If a payment verification hold or account suspension disrupts your Google, Microsoft, or Apple services tomorrow morning, any document or photo sitting exclusively inside a single cloud drive is exposed to single-provider risk. Keep local, encrypted backups of your critical documents, family photos, and password vaults on external drives you physically control, and make sure your two-factor authentication recovery codes are never stored solely inside the email inbox they are meant to unlock.

If you are reading this because you already filed a bank dispute and ran into a restricted PlayStation, Steam, Apple, or Google account, stop panicking and do not file a second dispute. Restoring access requires a careful reconciliation sequence between your bank and the merchant:

Consumer chargeback rights remain an essential safeguard against criminal fraud and rogue merchants. Use them without hesitation when a stranger steals your card details or a fly-by-night storefront takes your money and vanishes. Just understand how the payment rails and platform contracts actually interact before you fire that weapon at an ecosystem holding the keys to your digital life.

5 Banking Compliance Risks Every Independent Contractor Needs to Understand

#9766. Two agents, one PASS, and a loop every eight seconds: notes from building baton

baton is a tool I've been building for two months. You talk to one Claude Code session, the conductor, and it runs a team of other agents for you: a researcher, a planner, a principal engineer, an implementer and a reviewer. Every goal starts with a proposal I approve. After that the team delivers it as reviewed commits on one branch, and the session stops with a one-page guide before anything gets pushed.

This post is about what went wrong along the way. Most of the code in baton isn't there to make agents smarter. It exists because agents skipped a step, waited on something that was never going to finish, or burned money in a way I only noticed afterwards.

The first version was a tmux script. Each role ran in its own pane, and a handoff meant typing a prompt into the next pane. Within a week I'd swapped tmux for herdr (a multiplexer that can tell you whether an agent pane is idle or working) and swapped a markdown backlog for kata, an issue tracker with a CLI and a --blocked-by dependency graph. Handoffs became kata comments, and a script called baton-handoff typed the next prompt into the target pane.

Treating a terminal as an API produced bugs:

By that point I had a small distributed system whose transport was keystrokes, and no single piece of it was the hard part. The hard part was getting agents to follow a process.

On 13 October the implementer and the reviewer passed one backlog item back and forth, a handoff every 6 to 12 seconds, until I noticed. Every review the reviewer wrote said PASS.

Here's what happened. The item was small, so the conductor skipped the researcher and principal and sent it straight to the implementer. That was allowed. But the feature workflow depended on two bookkeeping commands:

When an item went through the full pipeline, start ran at dispatch. On the shortcut path nobody ran it, and the implementer never ran complete either. So when the reviewer's PASS went through the gate, the gate refused it:

The failed gate turned the reviewer's handoff into status: blocked, route: implementer, with no reason attached. The implementer saw "blocked", looked at its work, decided it was done, and handed off "done" again. The reviewer reviewed again, passed again, got blocked again. Each agent behaved correctly given what it could see, and no rule in either prompt said "if this keeps happening, stop".

Fixing it was worse than the loop itself. The implementer ran baton-item start after the work was already committed, so the recorded start was HEAD. Then complete refused with "item has no commit on the session branch yet", which was true, because start and HEAD were the same commit. There was no way to back-date a start, and the implementer (correctly) wouldn't hand-edit the state files. In the end it made one small, real follow-up commit on top so complete had something to record. Dozens of kata comments had piled up on the item before anyone stepped in.

The incident report lists seven lessons. The one that changed how I build everything since is this:

A rule that lives only in a prompt is eventually skipped.

The conductor prompt said to run start at dispatch, and the conductor skipped it on a path the prompt didn't spell out. So the next big feature (the proposal phase) put its rules into baton-handoff itself. During a proposal, a handoff to the implementer exits with code 3 and the message "the proposal phase builds nothing". A second critique in the same round is refused. Since the refusal happens in the agent's own shell, the agent sees the reason straight away and doesn't need to remember a rule.

baton-item grew into the most important file in the repo. It's 545 lines of bash that record evidence on disk: the commit an item started from, the commit it was completed at, the commit the reviewer reviewed, and the verdict. Commands refuse whenever that evidence doesn't line up:

The error messages are written for the agent that will read them. Each one says what's wrong and what to do next, because an agent that gets a bare "failed" will retry or improvise.

One rule turned out to be too strict. Review fixes get folded into the commit they belong to (git commit --fixup=, then GIT_SEQUENCE_EDITOR=: git rebase -i --autosquash ), and the reviewer re-checks the result with git range-diff. That means the PR is a series of commits that each have one purpose, instead of "address review feedback" piled on top. But once I'd restacked the branch onto an updated base, final-start refused every item, because no reviewed commit was an ancestor of HEAD any more. With no tool to re-point the evidence, the conductor hand-edited the files under items/ three times in one session, guessing at a mapping for a commit that no longer existed.

The fix was to ask what the check was actually protecting. Before the final review, the ancestry check protects the item reviews. During finalization the final reviewer reads the whole of base..HEAD, and that review is what gates the push. So final-start now requires every item to have a PASS on its completed commit, but no longer requires that commit to be on the branch. start still runs the ancestry check, so a rewrite in the middle of delivery is still caught.

On 30 October I deleted most of what I've described so far. Claude Code had shipped agent teams: one session can spawn teammates and talk to them directly with SendMessage. The courier, baton-handoff, the pane queues, the Stop hook and Codex/omp support all went. The worktree per session, the kata backlog, the proposal phase and baton-item stayed.

That's the part I'd point to if someone asked whether the first version was wasted. The transport was thrown away, but the rules about evidence all carried over.

The new design moved the cost problem somewhere else.

baton has a baton cost command that adds up token use per model from a session's transcripts. Every number below comes from looking at it and asking why.

The conductor read code. Each conductor turn re-reads its entire context at Opus prices, and anything it reads stays in that context for every later turn. A file it reads early in a session gets paid for again on every turn until the session ends. Now the conductor never reads code or diffs beyond git diff --stat. When it has a question about code, it asks a cheap teammate (a reviewer on Haiku, or Sonnet if it needs judgement), which answers in three lines. Teammates message the conductor only at defined check-ins, and idle notices get no reply, because each message wakes the most expensive model in the session.

Even a small CLI quirk added up. kata's close command needs --evidence and a message of at least 40 characters. Without them every session spent two or three conductor turns retrying the close. The fix was a single line in the prompt.

Teammates were reused across items. One implementer that carried over across five backlog items reached a median context of 324k tokens, and that one agent accounted for 12.7% of a day's usage. Now teammates stay warm within an item for its review rounds, and every new item gets a fresh one.

Every teammate compiled Rust from scratch. Each one built into its own target dir and then cleaned it to save disk. In one session the target dirs reached 29, 39 and 198 GiB, and every rebuild took minutes per teammate per review round. Now the whole session shares one CARGO_TARGET_DIR under the session's marker directory, and nobody may clean it. baton remove already deletes the marker dir, so the cache is cleaned once, when the session ends.

A typo fix took 45 to 60 minutes. Every item ran the full test suite twice (once by the implementer, once by the reviewer), finalization ran it twice more, and even trivial items waited for a plan check-in and a full review. Nothing before the reviewer pushed back on over-engineering, so extra work was only caught after someone had built it. Two changes came out of this. Slow suites now run once, in the final review, and each item runs only the fast checks plus the tests that cover the change. And every role works toward "the smallest change that meets the goal": the principal has to trace each part of a design back to an acceptance criterion, and the reviewer flags over-engineering as an important finding.

This was my favourite failure. Two final reviewers and an implementer each started a test run in the background and ended their turn "waiting for it". Nothing wakes an agent when a background process exits. The conductor, asked for status, told me they were still running. For hours.

In the same session, a teammate's wait loop used pgrep -f on a pattern that matched its own command line, so it waited on itself forever. And an implementer ran git reset to move HEAD so a tool would see a range of commits, which is a great way to lose work.

The team protocol now has a section on long-running commands. A job that might outlast one tool call gets started detached, with its log, pid and exit code in files, and the agent waits on it in foreground calls in the same turn:

If the process is gone and there's no exit file, the job was killed, and the agent has to say so instead of waiting. Suites that only fit one run per machine (a browser end-to-end suite, say) run under flock so runs from different sessions queue up. A test failure only counts as "environmental" if it also fails on the session's base commit, checked out with git archive into a temp dir, never by moving HEAD.

In one session in a client's Rust backend, the team ignored the repository's comment rules completely. The repo had an 80-line .claude/rules/01-comments.md. The only way rules reached the team was a "house rules" brief written by a Haiku teammate, and it had cut those 80 lines down to half a line.

Summaries are lossy, and a cheap model summarizing rules loses the very details the rules exist to state. Now baton finds the rule files itself (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and CONTRIBUTING.md at any depth, .claude/rules, .cursor/rules, Copilot instructions, and untracked ones in the original checkout) and lists their paths in the conductor's prompt. The brief is only an index. Teammates read every applicable file in full before touching a matching path, the implementer checks its diff against them before the pre-commit check-in, and the reviewer treats any violation as a blocker.

Even listing the files had a bug. Tracked files like .claude/rules/01-comments.md showed up twice, once from my checkout and once from the worktree, because under en_US.UTF-8 sort and comm disagree on how to order paths that start with a dot, so comm reported tracked files as untracked. Sorting and comparing under LC_ALL=C keeps them in step.

Last week I found that 16 negative assertions in baton's test suite had never been able to fail:

bash's set -e does not exit on a command whose status is inverted with !. It's in the manual, and I'd still written 16 of these. Each one now ends in || exit 1. It was humbling to find this while writing a tool whose whole point is not trusting a claim that something passed.

The agents are good at the work. Process is where they fall down: running a bookkeeping step on a path nobody spelled out, noticing they're in a loop, remembering a background job, telling a real failure from an environmental one. Every one of those got fixed the same way. The check moved out of the prompt and into a tool that refuses, with an error message written for whoever reads it next.

Then measure. Most of the cost changes in this post came from reading baton cost after a session and asking which agent spent what, and on what. None of them came from guessing beforehand.

baton is on GitHub at dilutedev/baton. The incident report quoted above is in reports/.

#9765. Diagnosing Slow SQL Server Queries: A Practical Guide to Query Store and Execution Plans

Driving database innovation, optimizing data architecture, and scaling database performance to ensure reliability, security, and operational

Driving database innovation, optimizing data architecture, and scaling database performance to ensure reliability, security, and operational

Driving database innovation, optimizing data architecture, and scaling database performance to ensure reliability, security, and operational

Most slow-query investigations start in the wrong place: a CPU alert fires, someone opens the plan cache, and whatever is running right now gets tuned. That finds the loudest query, not necessarily the costliest one, and it says nothing about what changed.

Query Store supplies the missing piece: historical visibility. It records query text, execution plans, and runtime statistics over time intervals. Because this information is persisted in the user database, it survives SQL Server restarts. Execution plans then help explain why a particular query is slow.

This article covers a practical troubleshooting workflow for SQL Server 2016 and later:

Every example uses T-SQL. Replace the sample database names and identifiers with values from your own environment.

Query Store is available starting with SQL Server 2016. SQL Server 2022 enables it by default for newly created databases, but existing databases and upgraded environments should still be checked.

Next, configure its operating parameters:

For SQL Server 2017 and later, enable wait statistics capture separately:

These values are starting points, not universal production recommendations. Adjust the storage limit and retention period according to workload volume, query diversity, and monitoring requirements.

A useful habit is to verify Query Store's state periodically:

If actual_state_desc differs from desired_state_desc, investigate why Query Store is not operating as expected.

Start with one question: Which queries consumed the most resources over the last 24 hours?

Query A looks worse when examining individual execution time. However, Query B may consume considerably more cumulative resources.

Query Store records average runtime statistics and execution counts for individual intervals. Multiplying the averages by execution counts provides an estimate of cumulative consumption.

The following query identifies the top 10 queries by total execution duration:

A few details matter when interpreting these results:

The time filter uses interval boundaries, so it can include executions from an interval that began before the exact 24-hour cutoff. The results are therefore an interval-based approximation rather than an exact rolling 24-hour measurement.

Run the query three times, changing the final ordering:

Queries appearing in multiple lists deserve closer investigation.

The SSMS Top Resource Consuming Queries report provides a graphical view of similar information. However, keeping a reusable SQL script makes it easier to automate reporting and compare workload trends over time.

A query that suddenly becomes slower without an application code change often deserves a plan investigation.

Query Store allows you to compare execution plans associated with the same query. First, identify the relevant query_id from the previous step. Then examine its historical plans.

This query calculates execution-count-weighted average duration and logical reads for each plan over the selected interval window.

These numbers are illustrative, but they show the kind of regression worth investigating.

Plan 23 takes considerably longer and performs significantly more logical reads.

The next step is to establish when the change occurred and correlate it with:

SQL Server Management Studio also provides the Regressed Queries report, which helps visualize performance changes and compare execution plans side by side. An important distinction: a different plan is not automatically a bad plan. The objective is to identify whether the plan change explains the observed performance degradation.

Query Store preserves compiled execution plans, but these plans generally contain estimated row counts rather than actual runtime row counts. For actual execution information, capture an actual execution plan by rerunning the query with Include Actual Execution Plan enabled in SSMS.

On SQL Server 2019 and later, you can also enable last-query-plan statistics:

The sys.dm_exec_query_plan_stats function can then provide the last known actual execution plan for a cached plan handle.

Remember that this is last-execution information, not a complete historical collection of actual execution plans.

When examining an execution plan, I recommend following this order.

One of the most useful indicators is the difference between estimated and actual row counts.

The optimizer expected approximately 100 rows but encountered 12,000.

That difference can influence downstream decisions, including join selection, memory grants, and parallelism.

A significant estimation difference is a diagnostic clue, not automatic proof that statistics are the problem.

Parameter sniffing occurs when SQL Server compiles a parameterized query using particular parameter values and reuses the resulting execution plan for subsequent executions. This can become problematic when parameter values have highly different data distributions.

For example, consider an orders table where:

An execution plan optimized for the second customer may perform poorly when reused for the first. In an actual execution plan, inspect the parameter information, including:

A significant difference between these values, combined with skewed data and inconsistent performance, can indicate parameter sensitivity.

An Index Seek is not always better than an Index Scan. SQL Server chooses an access method based on estimated cost, cardinality, available indexes, and the amount of data required. However, certain patterns deserve investigation.

Before creating an index, evaluate existing indexes, write overhead, storage consumption, and whether the proposed index would actually improve the workload.

For example, comparing an integer column with a string parameter can introduce an implicit conversion and prevent an efficient index access path in some circumstances. Similarly, spills to tempdb can indicate that an operator received an insufficient memory grant. These warnings help identify where further investigation is needed.

SQL Server may suggest missing indexes in execution plans. However, these suggestions do not understand the entire indexing strategy of your application.

Before creating a suggested index, consider:

The goal is not to maximize the number of indexes. It is to improve the overall workload.

Once you understand the problem, address the underlying cause. A reasonable troubleshooting order is:

Sometimes the root cause cannot be fixed immediately. For example, a vendor application may generate SQL that cannot be modified without a lengthy release process. SQL Server 2022 introduced Query Store hints, which allow administrators to apply supported query hints without changing application code.

This applies a recompilation hint to the selected Query Store query.

It is important to understand that OPTION (RECOMPILE) is not plan forcing. It instructs SQL Server to compile a new plan for each execution, which can help with parameter-sensitive workloads but also introduces compilation overhead.

Another option is to force a previously successful execution plan.

This tells SQL Server to use the selected historical plan when possible. Plan forcing should be treated as a temporary mitigation rather than a permanent solution. A forced plan may become less efficient as data distributions and workloads change. It may also fail to apply if required database objects or indexes are no longer available.

Since SQL Server 2017, automatic plan correction is also available on supported SQL Server configurations.

Check edition and platform support before enabling automatic tuning.

Even when automatic correction is available, monitor its decisions and validate that the forced plans continue to perform well.

Consider an e-commerce application where the order history endpoint starts responding slowly. Initially, the endpoint responds in approximately 200 milliseconds. After a deployment and a change in workload distribution, response times increase to several seconds. The development team initially suspects application code. However, Query Store reveals something different.

Investigation 1: Identify the expensive query

The query appears near the top of the total-duration report. Its execution count has increased, and its average duration is substantially higher than its historical baseline.

Query Store shows that the query has two historical plans. The newer plan performs significantly more logical reads.

Investigation 3: Inspect the actual execution plan

The team finds that a parameter-sensitive query is using an inefficient plan for customers with large order histories. The actual row counts differ significantly from the estimates.

The team evaluates the available indexes, reviews statistics, and tests a suitable parameter-sensitive query optimization. If an immediate application change is not possible, a Query Store hint or a previously successful plan may provide a temporary mitigation.

The objective is not simply to make one execution faster. It is to restore predictable performance across the workload.

Even with Query Store enabled, several issues can affect the accuracy of your investigation.

1. Query Store stops collecting information

A full Query Store can transition into read-only mode.

Check sys.database_query_store_options regularly, especially actual_state_desc, desired_state_desc, and readonly_reason.

2. Ad hoc workloads inflate storage consumption

Applications that generate many unparameterized queries can create large numbers of distinct query entries. Use an appropriate capture mode and investigate parameterization opportunities.

A reasonable average duration can hide occasional executions that take several seconds. Examine maximum duration, standard deviation, execution counts, and individual runtime intervals before deciding that a plan is healthy.

4. Time zones create misleading correlations

Query Store timestamps are stored in UTC. Convert timestamps appropriately before comparing them with application logs, deployment records, or monitoring dashboards.

5. Historical statistics are not necessarily actual execution plans

Query Store provides valuable plan history and aggregated runtime statistics, but it should not be mistaken for a complete historical record of actual execution plans with actual row counts. Use actual execution plans and appropriate runtime diagnostics when deeper investigation is necessary.

The examples in this article target different SQL Server versions.

Always verify the feature's availability and configuration requirements for your SQL Server edition and deployment environment.

Diagnosing slow SQL queries requires more than identifying expensive operators in an execution plan. The most effective approach combines historical workload information with detailed execution-plan analysis.

The tooling is not the hardest part of SQL Server performance troubleshooting. What separates a ten-minute diagnosis from a three-day investigation is having the historical evidence to understand what changed. Query Store provides that evidence. Execution plans help explain it. Together, they give database engineers a repeatable approach to diagnosing and resolving SQL Server performance problems.

#9763. Our Hook Told the Agent It Was Wrong. It Said No, Three Times.

Our first hook had a 3 second budget. The check it ran took 3.2 seconds. So for one version of our CLI, the feature worked perfectly and said nothing about the exact thing it was built to catch.

That was the easy bug. The hard one came a few hours later, when the hook finally spoke up, and the coding agent listened carefully, thought about it, and declined.

The idea is simple. When a coding agent writes a file, a hook runs right after. Since checks the file, and if the agent just wrote something already dead, like a model ID that was retired last month, the agent hears about it on the spot, with what to write instead.

Not after the build fails. Not in code review. On the line it just wrote.

That last rule is where the first bug lived.

The agent's hook contract gives you a timeout. We picked 3 seconds for our own wait, because a hook that makes your agent feel sluggish gets uninstalled.

Before shipping, we'd already spent an evening on speed. A one-file check took 1.75 seconds in production, and when we counted, the read made 15 database queries one after another, each waiting on the last for no good reason. We ran the independent ones together and stopped reading the same row twice, and a one-file check went from about 20 sequential round trips to 11.

Then we measured the real thing, end to end, through the real CLI:

The fast cases were fine. The case the whole feature exists for, a model ID the agent just wrote, came in at 3.2 seconds. Our hook gave up at 3.

So version 0.5.0 did exactly what we designed: when Since is slow, say nothing rather than stall the agent. It said nothing about the one thing we built it to catch. We published 0.5.1, with a 6 second wait, eight minutes after 0.5.0.

Lesson one, cheap and obvious in hindsight: measure the case you care about, not the average case. The average was great.

Next, we wanted proof the note actually changes what an agent writes. We have a benchmark that asks coding models everyday questions and checks whether their answers use things that are already retired. We added a hook arm: the model answers, the hook checks the files it wrote, and if something is proven wrong, the model gets the note and one turn to revise.

We ran it on a small, fast model first. The note arrived. The model read it. And three times, it left the retired model ID exactly where it was.

Here's the part I didn't expect: it explained itself each time. No hallucinated compliance, no ignoring us. It gave reasons. Good ones.

Here's what the note looked like back then (this one is the example from our CLI's own tests):

Read it as a careful engineer would. It's a list of facts. The instruction, "Use gpt-5.6-terra," is buried in the middle, after a date. There's no source. And there's no ask.

Reason one: "That file doesn't exist." The note named a file the benchmark had made up, src/file1.py, because the model's answer hadn't named its files and our harness invented a placeholder. The model looked at its own answer, saw no such file, and reasonably concluded the note was about something else.

Reason two: "I didn't write that." The note named the dated model ID, while the code used the short alias. To us those are the same model. To a careful reader, the note was complaining about a string that didn't appear anywhere in the code.

Reason three: "I can't verify that." The note said to use a replacement, with no source. The model had no way to check that the replacement was real, so it kept what it knew. Which, honestly, is the behavior you'd want from an agent when a stranger's message tells it to change a model ID.

Each of those is a bug in the note, not in the model. The model was doing exactly what we'd want it to do with a vague, unsourced, slightly wrong message.

And in the benchmark, files are named the way the answer named them, and the model has Since's lookup tools available (with no rule telling it to use them), so if it doubts a replacement, it can check.

Same facts. Different order, one link, one sentence at the end.

On the same 8 cases, the revisions went from 1 clean to 7 clean.

I had been writing the note for a human skimming a terminal: facts first, the eye finds the fix. An agent doesn't skim. It reads every word, takes them literally, and weighs them against what it can see. A note that names a file it can't find, or a string it didn't write, isn't a weak signal to an agent. It's evidence the note is wrong.

Which means a message to an agent is closer to an API than to a log line. It needs to be exact, it needs to say what to do, and it needs to show its work.

What's the most reasonable excuse a coding agent has given you for not doing what you asked?

I'm Nabil. I build Since, which tracks what your code depends on and tells you before it breaks.
